ety.text: From Middle English tissu, from Old French tissu (“woven”), past participle of tistre (“to weave”), from Latin texō (“to weave”).

senses.d: A fine transparent silk material, used for veils, etc.; specifically, cloth interwoven with gold or silver threads, or embossed with figures.
ex: A Robe of Tiſſue, ſtiff with golden Wire; / An upper Veſt, once Hellen’s rich Attire; [...]
In their glittering tissues bear emblazed / Holy memorials.

senses.d: A sheet of absorbent paper, especially one that is made to be used as tissue paper, toilet paper or a handkerchief.
A group of cells (along with their extracellular matrix if any) that are similar in origin and function together to perform a specific job.
ex: What they lack is outermost brain tissue that, at least in humans, prompts awareness and interpretation.

senses.d: Web; texture; complicated fabrication; connected series.
ex: a tissue of forgeries, or of lies
unwilling to leave the dry bones of Agnosticism wholly unclothed with any living tissue of religious emotion

senses.d: The scratch sheet or racing form.
ex: Lenehan came ourt of the inner office with Sport's tissues. —Who wants a dead cert for the Gold cup? he asked.

senses.d: Anything that is light, thin, and delicate.
To form tissue of; to interweave.
ex: The Chariot was couered with Cloth of Gold tiſſued vpon blew.

senses.d: To have the contents of an injection or intravenous drip leak into the tissue as a result of a ruptured or punctured vein.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French tissu, participle of tistre (modern tisser). Compare Italian tessuto.

it:tessuto.gl: textile, fabric, material, stuff, cloth, weave

ety.text: Past participle of tessere. Cognate with Piedmontese tëssù.
From tejer (“to weave”) + -ido. Compare English tissue.
Past participle of tecer (“to weave”), from Old Galician-Portuguese tecer, from Latin texere (“to weave”). Cognate of texto (“text”).
